components.text: Whether religious belief has rational support beyond its proposed psychological origin in fear and consolation.
The decisive demand is whether religious belief is better explained as fear-driven human projection than as disclosure of a real deity.
Whether natural inquiry adequately explains the relevant world and whether observed history supports a providential plan.
Whether describing God as the source of existence provides a necessary or well-supported explanation.
The decisive inference is that unexplained existence and significant intangible phenomena make a purposive theistic explanation reasonable.
The additional demand is whether a source of existence is also warranted as a purposeful relational God.
Whether verifiable natural cosmology and evolution remove the explanatory need for a providential deity.
Whether belief in God is better explained as fear-driven parental projection.
The decisive relevant component is whether a material natural account adequately explains intentional human freedom rather than only biological history.
Whether material human origins entail complete predetermination and therefore require immaterial God-grounded agency.
The decisive demand is whether material origins make every human act predetermined and therefore require an immaterial divine source of freedom.
Whether religious belief is a fear-driven projection rather than truth-directed disclosure.
Whether natural explanation and destructive history undermine providential religion.
Whether material contingency answers the immaterial-agency argument.
The legal earlier demand is whether religion is a fear-driven human projection whose consoling function supplies no truth warrant.
A further demand concerns whether natural explanations and destructive history undermine providential religious purpose.
Whether the tradition's claimed orientation toward justice and character withstands the content of foundational religious laws.
Whether scripture and religious alignment plausibly disclose a purposive divine source.
The decisive claim is that Judaism's central ethical purpose adequately distinguishes the tradition from abuses committed under religious authority.
Whether inherited scriptural defects establish religion's enduring moral character and negate its capacity to direct justice.
The decisive demand is whether inherited scriptural defects show a uniquely divine source is absent and continue to compromise religious moral authority.
Whether religion supplies a distinctive moral capacity or action unavailable without faith.
Whether a refining religious system contributes morally distinctive conduct.
The decisive earlier claim is that Judaism's teachings and practices direct adherents toward justice and character refinement despite abuses.
A further claim is that religious traditions can morally improve by revising inherited defects.
Whether the absence of uniquely available religious acts exhausts religion's possible moral contribution.
Whether religious practices are merely fear-driven consolation rather than meaningful experiences.
The decisive challenge asks whether religion enables any genuinely good act or moral statement that an unbeliever cannot perform.
Whether religious consolation is merely fear-driven illusion rather than a meaningful human response.
Whether religion contributes anything significant beyond capacities available to unbelievers.
The decisive demand is whether religious consolation is merely a fear-driven projection whose emotional usefulness does not establish truth.
Whether evolving religious traditions sufficiently neutralize the conflict and coercion produced by claims of divine authority.
Whether religion's orientation toward justice outweighs authority-dependent harms.
Whether religious motivation is reliably beneficial rather than capable of motivating violence.
The decisive claim is that religion's central ethical orientation distinguishes it from abuses of governmental or religious authority.
The additional claim is that evolving religious systems can discard inherited moral dross and make people better.
Whether divine or religious motivation is needed to furnish substantive moral direction.
Whether religious tradition uniquely directs decent conduct and justice.
Whether practical religious meaning establishes a superior moral framework.
The decisive relevant claim is that religious teaching supplies an ethical framework directing people toward decent reciprocal conduct.
An additional demand is whether religious framing contributes something necessary or distinctive to moral practice.
Whether contextual ethical reasoning can preserve real right and wrong without a transcendent foundation.
Whether unbelievers' moral capacity makes divine grounding unnecessary.
The decisive demand is whether shared reciprocal norms and contextual reasoning suffice without a transcendent source of objective right and wrong.
An additional demand distinguishes unbelievers' moral ability from any unique role claimed for faith.
Whether calling God the source of existence explains origins and establishes a relational religious deity.
Whether evidence for intangible reality establishes the specifically theistic conclusion.
The decisive inference is that existence and intangible realities reasonably support belief in God as their transcendent explanation.
The additional claim identifies God as the source of everything and a relational ground of purposeful life.
Whether profound experiences of meaning, mortality, and consolation warrant a supernatural interpretation.
Whether love, consciousness, and intangible experience support theism.
Whether numinous and sanctified experience is uniquely religious.
The decisive inference is that consciousness, love, meaning, and intangible experience make a supernatural or theistic ground reasonable.
An additional claim is that religion distinctively supplies experiences of sanctity and transcendent emotional meaning.
A further claim is that religious meaning and consolation disclose more than ordinary natural experience.
Whether shared reciprocal norms and contextual reasoning can make moral obligation universally binding.
Whether nonbelievers' ability and motivation to act morally eliminate the need for transcendent authority.
The decisive challenge is whether an unbeliever lacks any capacity to perform a genuinely good act or state a moral truth.
An additional demand is whether shared norms and contextual reasoning adequately ground universally binding obligation.
Whether evolutionary randomness and contingency explain intentional human choice rather than merely defeating strict predetermination.
Whether asking what caused God generates a fatal regress for the theistic agency account.
The decisive demand is whether evolutionary contingency and random mutation defeat the need for an immaterial account of intentional human choice.
An additional challenge asks whether appealing to a divine chooser merely relocates the explanatory regress.
